notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material on Psalm 13 from the older commentaries, from Enduring Word, and from Augustine. But **I found no source where Protestant traditions actually disagree about this psalm**, and the disagreements that do show up are between individual commentators. I also found nothing from NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Orthodox sites, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm, so those parts are left out.

## Whole psalm (overview)
- Maclaren (Expositor's Bible) splits it into three parts. Verses 1–2 are a complaint from someone at the end of his strength. Verses 3–4 are a prayer that keeps a weak faith going. Verses 5–6, which are one in the Hebrew, is the voice of confidence, which in the midst, of trouble, makes future deliverance and praise a present experience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/13.htm
- Ellicott thinks it may come from the years when David was running from Saul. However, Psalm 13:3 sounds rather like the cry of one suffering from sickness. All we can be certain about is that the psalm is intense in its record of personal feeling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/13.htm
- Guzik calls it a psalm of transition: it starts in discouragement and despair and ends in trust and joy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-13/

## v. 1
- **Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary says God cannot forget, but man often feels as if he were forgotten of him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/13.htm
- Guzik: God did not really forget David or hide from him, but David felt that He had. What David felt was true to his feelings, not to the facts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-13/
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** The fourfold "How long?" shows how badly David wanted rescue. Spurgeon admits some impatience may be mixed in, and warns that it is not easy to prevent desire from degenerating into impatience. He nicknamed it the "Howling Psalm." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps013.cfm
- **"How long... forever?":** Keil & Delitzsch see a fight inside him between the flesh and the spirit. The dejected heart thinks "forever," but the spirit turns that thought into a question, so that it only *seems* God has forgotten him. They quote Luther: "hope itself despairs and despair nevertheless begins to hope." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/13-1.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** David speaks from his own feelings, not from what other people thought of him. By bringing the complaint to God at all, he shows that faith was lifting him above what the flesh concluded. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-13.html
- Gill: God's "face" means His gracious presence. God sometimes withdraws it from His people as a response to their bad behaviour, but He still loves them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/13-1.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** God neither forgets nor turns His face away; Scripture speaks after our manner. His face being turned away means God has not yet given the soul knowledge of Himself. Augustine also reads "unto the end" (from the Latin text) as pointing to Christ. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801013.htm
- **Wesleyan (Seedbed):** The "how long" psalms make room in Scripture for lament and painful questions put to God. https://seedbed.com/how-long-o-lord-psalm-13/

## v. 2
- **"Wrestle / take counsel in my soul":** The Pulpit Commentary pictures David making plan after plan to escape, none of which work. It suggests the planning may happen at night. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-13.html
- Barnes: Feeling abandoned, David was forced to try to save himself without God's help, and that was part of his sorrow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/13-2.htm
- Guzik: Thinking things over within himself only led David to daily sorrow. The answer is to look to the LORD, not inward. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-13/
- **A sharper reading:** Ellicott suggests the line may mean "form plans against my soul," and says the next verse confirms the suspicion that suicide had been in the psalmist's mind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/13.htm
- **"Each day":** Calvin reads it as sorrow that came back afresh every day, rather than sorrow lasting "all day long." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-13.html
- **"My enemy":** The Pulpit Commentary thinks this is probably Saul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/13.htm Augustine reads the enemy as either the devil, or carnal habit (bad habits of the flesh). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801013.htm
- Maclaren notes the order of the complaints: God first, then himself, then the enemy last. He says that order is taught by faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/13.htm

## v. 3
- **"Consider me and respond":** Barnes says God had seemed to turn His face away, so David now asks Him to look at him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/13-3.htm The Pulpit Commentary: David will not let himself be "forgotten" and reminds God of him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/13-3.htm
- **"Give light to my eyes": readings differ.**
  - *Renewed strength:* Maclaren says the request is not for illumination of vision, but for renewed strength. Dying eyes are dull and returning health brightens them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/13.htm Bible Hub's summary agrees ("restore vitality," with 1 Samuel 14:27). https://biblehub.com/psalms/13.htm
  - *Spiritual sight:* Guzik takes it as asking God to clear away the fog of discouragement and give His wisdom, linking it to Ephesians 1:17–19. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-13/
  - *Catholic (Augustine):* The "eyes of the heart," which should not be closed by the pleasure of sin. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801013.htm
- **"Sleep in death":** Ellicott takes it literally: go to sleep and never wake. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/13.htm Guzik also applies it spiritually: spiritual sleep often leads to spiritual death (Ephesians 5:14). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-13/

## v. 4
- Guzik: David dreads the enemy gloating, and that makes him more determined not to be shaken. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-13/
- Maclaren: The argument is that God's honour is tied to rescuing His servant. That is a true thought but needs care: We must make very sure that God's cause is ours before we can be sure that ours is His. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/13.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** The ones who would gloat are the devil and his angels. They could not gloat over Job, because Job was not shaken in his faith. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801013.htm

## v. 5
- Ellicott: "But I" is emphatic ("but as for me"). Complete peace has replaced despair. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/13.htm
- **"Loving devotion" (chesed):** Bible Hub explains it as covenant love that never quits (Exodus 34:6). https://biblehub.com/psalms/13.htm Guzik: when you cannot trust anything else, trust God's mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-13/
- **"Salvation": readings differ.**
  - Barnes says it means rescue from his present troubles, not salvation in the next world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/13-5.htm
  - Gill reads it in light of Christ: trust not in one's own righteousness but in God's mercy shown in the redemption Christ brings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/13-5.htm
  - *Catholic (Augustine):* "Salvation" means Christ, the Wisdom of God. Standing firm should not be credited to oneself, or pride will knock you over. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801013.htm
- Maclaren: Nothing outside has changed; the complaint and prayer have tightened his grip on God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/13.htm

## v. 6
- The Pulpit Commentary: The cry of "How long?" becomes a song, because he already feels revived, and that revival assures him rescue is coming. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/13.htm
- Gill: God's goodness has come through both providence and grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/13-6.htm
- Spurgeon's comment (quoted on Bible Hub): this last line takes back the charge of forgetfulness made in verse 1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/13-5.htm
- **Wesleyan (Seedbed):** His circumstances have not changed and his prayers may still be unanswered, yet he remembers and trusts. The main lesson is never to forget in the dark what God showed you in the light. Seedbed also links the psalm to Christ in Gethsemane, trusting God through His silence. https://seedbed.com/how-long-o-lord-psalm-13/
- **Text note:** The Greek (LXX) and Latin (Vulgate) Bibles add a line, "I will praise the name of the Lord most high," which no Hebrew manuscript has. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/13.htm Augustine comments on it: "I will sing" is with the heart, and "I will chant" is with one's works. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801013.htm

## What was not found
- **Protestant traditions disagreeing:** The differences above (v. 2 on suicide, v. 3 on "light," v. 5 on "salvation") are between individual commentators. The Luther lines are quoted second-hand by other commentators, not taken from a Lutheran site. I did not find Wesley's own notes, Pentecostal sites other than Enduring Word, or any Lutheran or Anglican source on this psalm.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching:** Nothing tied to Psalm 13.
- **Modern scholarship and Orthodox readings:** Nothing from NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey or Orthodox sites.
